Hi Alice / Bob,

Thanks again for the time this morning — good discussion on the streaming use case and how you expect traffic to grow once the feature is in beta. Quick recap and a couple of asks so our SRE/SE teams can size a safe starting quota for the trial: 

- SLO targets you called out: p50 <= 120ms, p95 <= 450ms for synchronous responses; streaming sessions target end-to-end latency under 500ms for chunk delivery.
- Target launch concurrency: ~250 parallel requests across the fleet (worst-case spikes to ~1,000 for 15–30s).
- Typical request: ~120 tokens in + 250 tokens out (streamed).
- Adapters: clients use HTTP/1.1 keep-alive today; some teams can switch to HTTP/2 if needed.

Attached: redwood-rate-limit-summary.pdf (short explainer of how we count requests/tokens and typical quota shapes). Can you send a short CSV with your expected sustained qps and peak bursts per region? If you already have a traffic sample (synth or real), attach that — it helps us map to connection pooling and multiplexing guidance.

Next steps I propose: SE review (Karthik) to recommend initial quota, then Marissa and I will propose a trial quota and timeline. If safe, we’ll enable a 2-week elevated burst window during onboarding.

Thanks,
Rachel

Rachel — thanks for the clear recap. Per your ask, attached is a small sample of our expected traffic for week 1 of beta: acme-requested-qps.csv. Key notes:

- Sustained baseline: 180 qps (US-East), with geo failover to US-West.
- Expected daily spikes: up to ~900 qps (20–60s) during big user events.
- Streaming sessions: we expect ~40 concurrent long-poll streaming sessions during peak (each session sends keepalive heartbeats every 8–10s).
- Many clients are behind NATs and use connection pooling via our gateway, which typically maintains ~8 persistent connections per service instance.

Question for Redwood: do you enforce both token-based and request-based rate limits simultaneously? Our load balancer can do aggressive multiplexing but we want to avoid 429s during the spike windows. Also curious about recommended client-side concurrency (per-host connections) and whether HTTP/2 multiplexing is necessary for stable p95 under load.

Attaching the CSV for reference. Happy to jump on a short call if that helps.

Best,

Hi Alice — thanks for the CSV, that helps. A few technical clarifications and an initial recommendation based on the numbers you shared: 

1) Limits model: Redwood enforces both request-rate (requests/sec) and token-rate ceilings. For streaming, we also track concurrent streaming sessions as a separate soft quota. 429s can occur if any of those caps are hit.

2) Mapping your numbers: sustained 180 qps maps to ~ (assume 370 tokens/sec aggregate) under your token sizes. Spikes to 900 qps for 20–60s are significant; we recommend a burst policy rather than a hard quota at that level.

3) Client-side recommendations:
   - Use HTTP/2 (multiplexing) if you plan >8 logical streams per TCP connection; otherwise keep-alive + 8–16 connections per gateway instance is fine.
   - For streaming sessions: limit client concurrency to 25 simultaneous streaming sessions per instance to avoid head-of-line contention on worker threads.

4) Redwood suggested starting quotas (trial):
   - Request rate baseline: 250 rps (per account)
   - Burst window: +1000 rps for 60s (rate-limited to protect nodes)
   - Concurrent stream sessions soft cap: 100 (global across region), with monitoring and auto-throttle alerts at 75
   - Token rate: 120k tokens/minute (enough headroom for your projected size)

5) Operational notes: enable keepalive and connection reuse; prefer HTTP/2 between your gateway and Redwood for the beta if you can — it significantly reduces connection churn and improves p95 under burst.

I attached a short multiplexing proposal showing connection/concurrency tradeoffs. If this looks reasonable I can formalize a proposal (quota numbers + onboarding runbook) and Rachel/Marissa can route approvals.

- Karthik
